pedagogy.summary: At KS3 the solar-system picture is upgraded from 'eight planets orbit the Sun' to a structured, quantitative system: rocky inner planets and gas/ice giants separated by an asteroid belt; moons orbiting planets; comets on long elliptical paths; and — the conceptual payoff — an orderly relationship between a planet's distance from the Sun and its orbital period (farther planets move slower along longer paths, so their 'year' is far longer). The teaching challenge is overwhelmingly one of SCALE: the sizes of bodies and, far more brutally, the distances between them are impossible to draw to scale on a page, which is exactly why children carry wildly wrong mental models. Best practice therefore leans on scaled models (a walked or measured-out solar system) and on data-handling — comparing real numbers for size, distance, and orbital period rather than reciting facts. The taxonomy of bodies (planet vs dwarf planet vs asteroid vs comet) is best taught by the defining criteria (orbit-clearing, roundness, composition, orbit shape) rather than as a memorised list.
bestPractices: Build a scaled model of distance, not just size: pace out or measure a to-scale solar system (e.g. Sun at one end of a field/corridor) so children physically feel that the inner planets are bunched near the Sun and the outer ones are absurdly far — the intuition a textbook diagram destroys
Work from real data tables: have children plot or compare distance vs orbital period and discover the pattern (farther = longer year) themselves rather than being told it

Teach the body categories by criteria: a planet clears its orbit and is round; a dwarf planet is round but shares its orbital zone; an asteroid is a small rocky body (mostly in the belt); a comet is icy on a long elliptical orbit that grows a tail near the Sun
Anchor 'why they stay in orbit' to gravity (the Sun's gravitational pull holds the whole collection) so the structure is causal, not just descriptive
Use comparison and proportion talk throughout ('Neptune is about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth') to make the scale crosscutting concept explicit
keyRepresentations: Scaled solar-system model (distance-to-scale walk or corridor model) — the canonical way to convey real separations
Data table / graph of planet distance vs orbital period revealing the ordered relationship
Structural map of the solar system: inner rocky planets | asteroid belt | outer giants, with moons around planets and comet orbits sketched
Comparison chart of the four body types against their defining criteria (roundness, orbit-clearing, composition, orbit shape)
commonMisconceptions: The planets are evenly spaced and roughly comparable in the gaps between them (textbook diagrams imply this; distances actually grow enormously outward)
All the planets line up on the same side of the Sun / orbit at the same speed
The asteroid belt is a dense, dangerous field of tightly packed rocks (it is mostly empty space)
Pluto is a planet, or dwarf planets are just 'small planets' rather than a category defined by not clearing their orbit
A comet's tail always trails behind its direction of motion (it actually points away from the Sun, driven by solar wind/radiation)
Orbital period has nothing to do with distance / outer planets simply 'choose' to go slowly

learn.summary: For learners aged ~11-12, upgrade the solar-system picture from 'eight planets orbit the Sun' to a structured, quantitative system: rocky inner planets and gas/ice giants separated by an asteroid belt; moons orbiting planets; comets on long elliptical paths; and the conceptual payoff — an orderly relationship between a planet's distance from the Sun and its orbital period (farther planets travel longer, slower paths, so their 'year' is far longer). The central teaching challenge is SCALE: sizes and especially distances cannot be drawn to scale on a page, which seeds wildly wrong mental models. Lean on scaled distance models (a walked or measured-out solar system) and on real data tables for size, distance and period, and teach the body categories (planet, dwarf planet, asteroid, comet) by their defining criteria rather than as a memorised list.

activities.title: Run and reshape a solar system
feedback: If a learner expects outer planets to move faster, point to the simulation: Neptune creeps while Mercury races — the bigger orbit AND the slower orbital speed both lengthen the year.

When a learner chooses a larger orbital radius in the idealised circular-orbit model and the year-counter climbs, reinforce: 'In this model, a larger orbit means slower orbital speed and a longer year, which matches the distance–period pattern of the real planets.' Remind them that the model resets the orbit; it does not show what would happen if a real planet were dragged outward.
If a learner thinks the gaps between planets are roughly even, use the true-scale toggle: the inner planets bunch near the Sun while the outer ones are absurdly far apart.

If a learner imagines the planets lined up on the same side of the Sun, point to the running view: they sit at different points around their orbits and move at different speeds, so they are rarely aligned.
activities.rationale: The load-bearing idea is a dynamic relationship best seen in motion; an idealised circular-orbit interactive where the learner chooses an orbital radius and watches speed and year respond makes the distance–period pattern easy to see, while a scale view conveys separations that readable static diagrams usually distort. Live data readouts turn observation into evidence. The radius-setting interaction and the scale toggle are illustrations, not mandatory.

KS3 physics includes gravity forces between the Sun and planets and the main features/structure of the solar system.
learnerActions: Watch an animated top-down solar system in motion: observe Mercury whipping round several times while Jupiter has barely moved and Neptune looks almost frozen
Read a live data panel showing each planet's distance and the length of its 'year' as it ticks up with distance

In an explicitly idealised circular-orbit model, choose a larger orbital radius and let the model recalculate circular speed and orbital period. Observe the longer period; this resets the model’s orbit rather than showing what would happen if a real planet were suddenly dragged outward.
Toggle a 'true scale' distance view that zooms out until the inner planets shrink to a speck near the Sun, then describe how far apart the outer planets really are
activities.intendedInsight: Farther from the Sun means a bigger orbital path travelled more slowly, so a much longer year — a dynamic relationship the learner causes and observes rather than being told. Real distances grow enormously outward, unlike evenly spaced textbook diagrams.

activities.title: Pace out the real distances
feedback: If a learner is surprised how far they must walk to the outer planets, confirm this is the point: standard diagrams compress these distances and seed the misconception of even spacing.
At this distance scale, correctly scaled planets would be very small. They can share one honest scale, but may be hard to see; label enlarged planet symbols clearly if using them.
activities.rationale: A physically walked or measured model lets learners feel real separations that a page-sized diagram cannot readily convey, making the scale concept concrete. A page-sized diagram cannot show both size and distance at one shared scale while keeping planets readable, so standard diagrams usually enlarge planets or compress distances, which seeds scale misconceptions. (The scaled-model recommendation comes from an educator-activity source marked unverified; it is offered as a proposal, not as established comparative efficacy.)
sourceClaims: Scaled-distance models are the recommended way to convey the true separations in the solar system because standard diagrams cannot represent both size and distance to scale, seeding scale misconceptions.

MS-ESS1-3 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-3], using data from telescopes and spacecraft; assessment explicitly does NOT reward recalling facts about planet properties, favouring data analysis of scale.
learnerActions: Build a scaled-distance model: using a chosen scale, place the Sun at one end of a field or corridor and pace out or measure where each planet falls
Notice physically that the inner planets are bunched close together while the outer planets are strikingly far away

Compare distances proportionally, for example Neptune is about thirty times Earth’s average distance from the Sun. An optional flythrough can display a light-travel-time counter; label any time compression rather than implying light crosses the system instantly.

Discuss why a page-sized model cannot readily show recognisable planet discs and their distances at one readable scale. A true shared-scale model is possible, but the planets become tiny at a scale that fits the whole system.
activities.intendedInsight: The true separations in the solar system are vast and grow enormously outward; a readable page-sized diagram with visible planets usually distorts this, which is why mental models are often wrong.

activities.title: Plot distance against orbital period
feedback: If a learner says every planet takes 'about a year,' compare Mercury (88 days) with Neptune (~165 years) to break the assumption.
If a learner guesses outer planets are 'shorter, they move faster,' point out the data shows the opposite: both the larger orbit and the slower orbital speed lengthen the year.
If a learner knows outer planets take longer but can't say why, prompt them toward 'bigger orbit + slower motion = longer year.'
activities.rationale: Comparing and plotting real numbers makes the distance–period relationship an evidence-based discovery and supports the data-analysis emphasis of the standard, and gravity is the causal anchor for why bodies stay in orbit at all.

The solar system consists of the sun and a collection of objects — including planets, their moons, and asteroids — held in orbit around the sun by its gravitational pull (ESS1.B disciplinary core idea).
learnerActions: Work from a real data table of planet distance from the Sun and orbital period
Plot or line up distance against period and describe the pattern you find
Compare specific cases: Mercury takes about 88 days for one orbit while Neptune takes about 165 Earth years
Explain in your own words why outer planets have longer years (bigger path travelled more slowly) rather than just stating the fact
activities.intendedInsight: Learners discover for themselves the ordered relationship — farther = longer year — and can justify it, instead of reciting it.

activities.title: Sort bodies by their defining criteria
feedback: If a learner lists Pluto among the planets, explain it hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood, which is what distinguishes a dwarf planet from a planet.

If a learner uses 'asteroid' and 'comet' interchangeably, contrast them: asteroid = rock/metal, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comet = ice and dust on a long looping orbit that grows a tail near the Sun.
An ion tail is approximately antisolar; a dust tail can curve. Use the illustrated tail type and do not infer the comet’s travel direction merely from a tail as if it were a smoke trail.
If a learner pictures the asteroid belt as a dense, dangerous field of tightly packed rocks, clarify that it is mostly empty space with vast gaps between the bodies.
activities.rationale: Teaching categories by defining features lets learners classify novel bodies and helps dismantle the 'Pluto is the ninth planet' and 'asteroids and comets are the same' misconceptions. A sort activity can check and support classification, but it does not by itself elicit the spoken explanation, so the explanation and tail-direction prompts are included explicitly. A tap-to-reveal labelled map or lift-the-flap criteria cards can support the naming/criteria layer as a reference companion.
learnerActions: Sort mystery objects into planet / dwarf planet / asteroid / comet using criteria, not memory

For each, apply the defining tests: Does it orbit the Sun and is it round? Has it cleared its orbital neighbourhood? Is it a small rocky/metal body (mostly in the belt)? Is it icy on a long elliptical orbit that grows a tail near the Sun?
Explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet: round and orbiting the Sun, but it shares its orbital zone (hasn't cleared it) — the same class as Ceres and Eris

Compare a comet’s ion tail, which points approximately away from the Sun under the solar wind, with its often curved dust tail shaped by radiation pressure and the comet’s orbital motion. Neither should simply be treated as a trail left behind the comet.
activities.intendedInsight: The four body types are defined by criteria (orbit-clearing, roundness, composition, orbit shape), so categorisation is reasoning, not recall; dwarf planets are a distinct category, not just 'small planets.'

activities.title: Explain the orbit, then check your understanding
feedback: Full response: 'Neptune takes much longer — about 165 Earth years — because it travels a far bigger orbit and moves more slowly.' Affirm both the bigger path and the slower orbital speed.
Partial response (knows outer = longer but not why, or names bodies without distinguishing them): prompt for the mechanism or the defining criterion.
Gap response ('about a year, like Earth' or 'shorter, it moves faster'): return to the Mercury-vs-Neptune comparison and the simulation before re-testing.
activities.rationale: A two-tier prompt asking both the outcome and the reason separates a genuine rule from a guess and exposes the reversed 'outer = faster' intuition. Ordering, categorising and estimating check mastery; place such checks after the exploratory and model work, since recognition-style items verify understanding rather than building the dynamic scale intuition on their own.

learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic: Neptune is much further from the Sun than Earth — does Neptune take longer or shorter than a year to go once round the Sun, and why?
Order the eight planets by distance and give one distinguishing fact about each
Categorise a set of bodies into planet, dwarf planet, asteroid and comet, naming the deciding feature in each case
Estimate the relative orbital periods of two planets and justify which has the longer year
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state and justify that farther-from-Sun = longer period, and cleanly distinguish the four body types — demonstrating a rule, not a guess.

activities.title: Locate moons as natural satellites
feedback: If all round objects are called planets, compare Earth and its Moon and identify the satellite relationship.
Do not imply that every planet has moons, or give an undated total for rapidly updated moon counts.
activities.rationale: Restores the stated moon/satellite objective alongside the preserved planet, dwarf-planet, asteroid and comet tasks. This is a proposed activity, not an empirically validated design.
learnerActions: Use inset diagrams to identify Earth’s Moon and Mars’s moons Phobos and Deimos as natural satellites.
Distinguish a planet or dwarf planet from a natural satellite bound to and orbiting another body; show that dwarf planets can have moons too.
Explain why being round is not enough to make Earth’s Moon a planet, and compare a satellite view with the wider Sun-centred system.
activities.intendedInsight: Moons are natural satellites within the wider solar system; roundness and a location near the Sun are not sufficient to classify a body as a planet.

constraints: State whether sizes, distances or both use a common scale. A page-sized true-scale model makes planets tiny, so readable diagrams often enlarge body symbols; label those symbols as not to scale.

A static labelled map or criteria cards support naming and classification but cannot animate motion or the distance–period relationship; use them as reference companions alongside a model that shows motion.
Recognition/multiple-choice checks verify understanding but do not on their own build the dynamic scale and motion intuition; sequence them after exploratory and model-based work.

A free-viewpoint 3D flythrough can convey scale, the flatness of the ecliptic and comet-orbit inclination, but adds navigation overhead; the core distance–period relationship reads clearly in a planar top-down view, so reserve 3D for a scale/immersion experience rather than treating it as necessary.
An open in-role dialogue (e.g. chat with a planetary scientist) can add context but is a poor vehicle for the spatial scale and motion intuitions that are the core objective.
Teach categories by criteria (orbit-clearing, roundness, composition, orbit shape), not as a memorised list; dwarf planets are a distinct class, not 'small planets.'

Distinguish ion and dust tails when discussing direction: the ion tail is approximately antisolar, while dust tails often curve. Avoid an unconditional claim that every visible tail points exactly away from the Sun.
Note that the asteroid belt is mostly empty space with large gaps, not a dense field of tightly packed rocks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NASA/JPL scaled-distance source claim was marked verified:false in the source row; its recommendation to use scaled-distance models is retained as a proposal, not as established comparative efficacy between media.

Orbital figures used (Mercury ~88 days, Neptune ~165 Earth years, 'Neptune about 30 times farther than Earth') are drawn from the source row and are approximate; confirm exact values against a current data table before classroom use.

The original row asserted 3D 'adds nothing' to the core insight and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' the intuitions; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits, since catalog fit rankings do not establish universal necessity or impossibility claims.

The source's physical statement that outer planets 'also move more slowly' is retained; note that both effects (larger orbit and slower orbital speed) contribute to the longer period — neither alone should be presented as the sole cause.

Activity 'Sort bodies by their defining criteria' has sourceClaims [] because no source claim directly supports the classification-by-criteria teaching principle; it rests on the pedagogy best-practice guidance rather than a cited, verified source.

probeDeeper: Mercury takes 88 days and Neptune takes 165 years for one orbit. What does that tell you about distance and the length of a year?
What's the difference between a planet and a dwarf planet like Pluto?
Is a comet just an asteroid with a tail? What actually makes them different?
assess.correctAnswer: Neptune takes much LONGER — about 165 Earth years for one orbit. Planets further from the Sun have longer orbital periods because they travel a far bigger orbit and also move more slowly. Further out = longer year.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'all planets take about a year' / no link between distance and orbital period
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare Mercury (88 days) with Neptune (165 years): further from the Sun means a bigger path travelled more slowly, so a much longer year.
errorPatterns.distractor: About the same — every planet takes roughly a year.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says Neptune takes roughly a year, the same as Earth

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Pluto is the ninth planet' (pre-2006 / dwarf-planet confusion)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pluto is a dwarf planet — it orbits the Sun and is round but hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood; same class as Ceres and Eris.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists Pluto among the planets or insists it still counts as one

errorPatterns.pattern: 'asteroids and comets are the same thing' (small-body conflation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Asteroid = rock/metal, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comet = ice and dust on a long looping orbit that grows a tail near the Sun.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all planets take about a year / no distance–period relation; treats Pluto as a planet and asteroids and comets as the same.
responseLevels.full: States further-from-Sun = longer orbital period and explains it (bigger, slower orbit), and cleanly distinguishes planet, dwarf planet, asteroid and comet with a defining feature each; transfers to ordering two planets' years.
responseLevels.partial: Knows outer planets take longer but can't say why, or names the bodies without distinguishing planet, dwarf planet, asteroid and comet.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Neptune is much further from the Sun than Earth is. Does Neptune take longer or shorter than a year to go once round the Sun — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with no distance–period relation says Neptune takes 'a year' like Earth, or guesses 'shorter, it moves faster.' A child who understands the relationship says 'much longer' and explains the bigger, slower orbit. The why-tier separates a real rule from a guess, and exposes the reversed 'outer = faster' intuition.
